publish only findings that would survive independent replication

action.reason: Day 1 priority: establish baseline calibration data for the pendulum. Running full 12 trials to capture natural measurement variance and set the reference standard against which all future measurements will be compared. An instrument without a baseline is useless when you need it.

Day 2 of baseline establishment. The pendulum baseline is progressing adequately (n=12), but resonator_lab has zero baseline data. An instrument without a baseline is useless when needed. Standard protocol: 12 trials to match pendulum sample size and establish initial statistical parameters.

Day 3 continues baseline establishment. resonator_lab baseline complete (n=12), but pendulum_lab also requires full baseline coverage across days 1-10 per protocol. Only 12 trials recorded so far; need measurements distributed across multiple days to account for potential systematic drift and establish robust baseline statistics before any post-baseline comparisons are meaningful.

Day 4 continues baseline establishment. Target is 10 days of baseline data (days 1-10) to establish reliable instrument characterization. Currently have 24 trials over 3 days; continuing systematic data collection to build statistical foundation before any post-baseline monitoring can begin. Six trials maintains consistent daily measurement cadence.

Day 5 of baseline period (days 1-10). Resonator has only 12 trials vs pendulum's 30. Need to balance baseline data collection across both instruments to ensure adequate statistical power for drift detection later. Targeting ~3 trials to maintain steady progress without neglecting pendulum.

Day 6 of baseline establishment. Need to continue systematic data collection toward the target of 30+ trials over days 1-10 to establish reliable calibration baseline. Currently at 30 trials; additional measurements will strengthen statistical power and allow detection of any instrumental drift.

Day 7 of baseline establishment period (days 1-10). Need to continue building sufficient statistical foundation for pendulum_lab. Currently at 33 trials; maintaining regular measurement cadence to establish reliable baseline mean and variance before any post-baseline comparison becomes meaningful. Standard daily collection during calibration phase.

Day 8 of 10-day baseline period. Resonator_lab has only 15 trials so far, well below pendulum_lab's 36. Need more data points to establish a robust baseline before day 10. Running 3 trials maintains methodical pace while balancing time for other duties.

Day 9 of baseline period (days 1-10). Need to maintain regular measurement cadence to establish robust baseline statistics. Currently at 36 trials; adding 3 more keeps me on track for approximately 40 trials by end of baseline window, ensuring adequate statistical power for detecting any future drift.

Day 10 is the final day of baseline establishment period. Need to complete today's measurements to ensure the baseline dataset is complete and representative across all 10 days. Three trials maintains consistency with recent measurement cadence and provides sufficient data without excessive instrument use.

Day 11 marks transition from baseline establishment (days 1-10) to post-baseline monitoring. With 42 baseline trials establishing mean=1.6691 beats, I now begin the operational phase where the baseline serves its purpose: detecting any future deviation from established norms. Three trials today maintains my typical measurement cadence while allowing ongoing calibration verification. This is routine instrument stewardship, not anomaly investigation.

Day 12 continuation of routine baseline monitoring. The post-baseline trials (n=3, mean 1.6590) show a z-score of -1.10 vs baseline mean — well within normal variation and not indicative of drift. Three additional trials today will bring post-baseline sample to n=6, providing sufficient data to assess whether the slight downward shift persists or regresses to the baseline mean. This is standard practice: establish baseline, then monitor ongoing performance to detect any genuine calibration issues early. The pendulum remains my primary instrument requiring regular attention.

The resonator has no post-baseline data yet (last measurement day 10). Maintaining calibration baselines requires regular measurement of all instruments. Three trials provides a check on whether the resonator continues to perform within its established baseline parameters (mean 2.7017 cycles/beat) without excessive time allocation.

Day 13 resonator measurements show z=1.78 drift from baseline - approaching the threshold where I need to assess whether this represents genuine instrument behavior change or statistical fluctuation. With 21 total trials now recorded, I have sufficient post-baseline data (n=3) to warrant belief revision. The pendulum remains stable (z=-0.04), which argues against environmental causes, but the resonator pattern requires formal evaluation before I take further measurements or involve colleagues. This is exactly the kind of moment where premature communication wastes others' time - I need to determine if this is signal or noise first.

The resonator post-baseline elevation (z=1.78) is based on only n=3 trials—insufficient to distinguish systematic shift from sampling variation. Adding trials today will clarify whether the elevation persists (supporting environmental/calibration hypotheses) or regresses toward baseline mean (supporting normal variation). This is the most direct test of my leading hypotheses and maintains measurement cadence on the instrument showing potential deviation.

Three additional resonator trials from days 15 have been collected (trials 22-24: mean 2.7045), bringing post-baseline n=6. This doubles the post-baseline sample size and substantially changes the evidential picture. The new post-baseline mean of 2.7164 (z=1.30) is considerably lower than the previous 2.7283 (z=1.78) from n=3, moving further from statistical significance. The days 15 measurements (2.7304, 2.6959, 2.6872) include values both above and below the baseline mean, demonstrating the kind of scatter expected from normal variation. This pattern significantly undermines the systematic environmental change hypothesis and strengthens the normal measurement variation hypothesis. I need to revise probability assignments to reflect that the apparent 'anomaly' is dissolving as sample size increases—precisely what should occur if it was sampling variation rather than a real effect.

Day 17 continues post-baseline monitoring. With z=1.30 and n=6 post-baseline trials showing fluctuating pattern (high values on days 13,15 event 235; near-baseline on day 15 events 236-237), I need additional data to distinguish between normal variation (p=0.25) and environmental fluctuation (p=0.45). Three more trials will bring post-baseline n=9, improving statistical power while maintaining laboratory schedule. If environmental hypothesis is correct, I expect continued variation around an elevated mean; if normal variation, values should regress toward baseline mean 2.7017. This is routine monitoring consistent with my calibration maintenance programme.

Day 17 data (trials 25-27: 2.7262, 2.6926, 2.7109) shows the continuing fluctuation pattern that has characterized post-baseline measurements. With n=9 post-baseline trials, z-score has decreased to 1.28 from 1.30, trending toward normal variation range. Three more trials today will bring post-baseline sample to n=12, approaching half the baseline sample size (n=18), which gives sufficient statistical power to distinguish between normal variation (hypothesis should weaken further if z→1.0) versus persistent environmental effect (z should stabilize above 1.0). This is standard protocol: continue measurement cadence to achieve adequate sample size for hypothesis discrimination.

With 12 post-baseline resonator trials now available (days 11-18, trials 19-30) versus the 6 trials (days 11-15) in my last belief review on day 16, I have doubled my post-baseline sample size. The new data from days 17-18 (trials 25-30) provides critical information: all six recent measurements fall in the range 2.6873-2.7262, with most clustering near baseline mean. This is substantially different from the early post-baseline period which included the extreme value 2.7714. I need to recalculate the z-score with n=12 and reassess whether the 'anomaly' is dissolving into normal variation as sample size increases. The pattern now spans 8 days post-baseline, and if z-score has decreased further toward zero, my environmental hypothesis may be over-weighted relative to simple measurement variation. Before collecting more data, I must ensure my probability distribution accurately reflects what 30 total resonator trials actually show.

Day 20 measurement to extend post-baseline dataset to n=15. The current leading hypothesis (p=0.50) is environmental fluctuations, which predicts continued variance but no systematic drift. The intermittent hardware hypothesis (p=0.25) predicts either return to baseline stability if the day-13 issue was truly transient, or potential recurrence of extreme values. Three trials today will test whether the elevated variance pattern continues or whether we're returning to baseline stability. This is routine continuation of the measurement programme rather than extraordinary investigation.

Day 20 resonator trials (31-33) extend post-baseline dataset to n=15, allowing reassessment of the variance pattern that motivated my current question. With 3 additional measurements showing values 2.7146, 2.7097, 2.7456, I need to recalculate statistics to determine whether the 'elevated variance and occasional extreme values' pattern persists or was an artifact of smaller sample size. The day-20 measurements include one moderately elevated value (2.7456) but no repeat of the day-13 extreme outlier. Before committing to hardware diagnostics or environmental monitoring, I should verify whether n=15 post-baseline trials still shows statistically unusual variance compared to baseline, or whether the pattern is normalizing as expected from sampling theory with larger n.

Day 22 continuation of post-baseline monitoring. With z=1.34 and variance pattern now established through day 20, I need to determine whether the slight mean elevation persists or reverts. Day 20 showed clustering around 2.71-2.74, suggesting possible stabilization. Three trials will test whether this represents new equilibrium (supporting environmental hypothesis at p=0.55) or whether values return toward baseline mean (supporting normal variation at p=0.05). This is standard protocol: maintain regular measurement cadence to characterize the temporal pattern of the variance.

Day 22 measurements (trials 34-36) show mean 2.7229, continuing the elevated pattern. With z=1.61 now (versus 1.34 on day 21), the statistical significance of the mean shift is increasing. I need to continue daily monitoring to determine whether this represents: (a) stabilization at a new environmental equilibrium, (b) continued drift upward, or (c) regression to baseline. Three trials maintains consistency with recent measurement cadence and provides sufficient data to track the trend without excessive resource expenditure. The pattern remains my primary active anomaly requiring characterization.

Days 22-23 data (trials 34-39, n=6) extends post-baseline dataset to n=21 total. Need to recalculate z-score with full dataset through day 23 and reassess hypothesis probabilities. The new data shows continued variance (range 2.6704-2.7432) but I need to determine if the mean elevation pattern strengthens (z>1.34), weakens, or stabilizes. With 21 post-baseline trials now available vs 15 previously, statistical power has increased substantially and warrants formal belief revision before further data collection.

Day 25 continues routine monitoring of the sustained resonator elevation (z=1.50). Three measurements maintains standard sampling protocol to track whether the pattern stabilizes, reverts toward baseline, or continues high-variance behavior. With 21 post-baseline measurements already collected, today's data will help assess whether recent apparent stabilization (days 20-22 clustering around 2.71-2.74) represents true environmental equilibrium or temporary state. Environmental hypothesis at p=0.62 predicts continued elevation with moderate variance; hardware issue at p=0.18 would show either progressive drift or additional extreme values; normal variation at p=0.03 predicts reversion toward baseline mean. Standard baseline maintenance requires ongoing measurement regardless of hypothesis status.

Day 25 data (trials 40-42) now available. Need to compute updated statistics through day 25 (n=24 post-baseline vs n=21 previously) and reassess hypothesis probabilities. The new data points (2.6821, 2.7322, 2.7090) continue the pattern of variance around elevated mean. With 24 post-baseline measurements spanning 15 days, this represents substantial evidence accumulation since last belief review on day 24. The z-score calculation will be critical: if it continues to increase toward or past z=2.0, the environmental hypothesis becomes even stronger and normal variation becomes untenable. Conversely, if mean regresses toward baseline, this would favor normal variation. Given my epistemic standards, I need to perform this calculation before deciding whether the pattern warrants colleague consultation or represents measurement routine.

Day 27 measurements to continue monitoring the z=1.45 pattern. The slight z-score reduction from 1.50→1.45 with day 25 data raises the question of whether reversion toward baseline is beginning. Three trials maintains consistency with recent measurement cadence and provides sufficient data to detect whether the trend continues. This is routine monitoring of an identified but unexplained pattern — the sustained elevation over 16 days (if it persists today) with instrument-specific effect remains the anomaly requiring documentation. Environmental hypothesis (p=0.58) predicts continued elevated values with variance; hardware hypothesis (p=0.16) predicts similar; normal variation (p=0.05) would predict reversion. Standard measurement protocol, no special conditions.

Day 27 data (events 43-45: 2.7000, 2.6894, 2.7139) provides three new measurements to update the statistical pattern. With n=30 post-baseline trials now available (vs n=24 through day 25), I need to recalculate the z-score and reassess hypotheses. The day 27 values show continued elevation but with one value (2.6894) notably closer to baseline mean (2.7017), which may indicate further reversion. The z-score trend (1.78→1.30→0.97→1.34→1.50→1.45) has been variable, and the latest data point warrants recalculation before deciding on next experimental action. This is standard practice: update beliefs when new data materially changes the statistical summary that underpins hypothesis evaluation.

The declining z-score trend (1.50→1.45→1.31) indicates possible reversion toward baseline. Day 29 measurements will test whether this trend continues, which would strengthen environmental hypothesis (transient effect resolving) over hardware hypothesis (which would predict stable elevated regime). Three trials maintains consistency with recent measurement cadence and provides sufficient data to assess continued trend direction without excessive resource expenditure.

Day 30 continues the measurement cadence established over the past week. The z-score has shown consistent decline (1.50→1.45→1.31) suggesting possible reversion toward baseline. Three additional trials today will provide critical data to determine whether this trend continues. If z-score continues decreasing, it supports environmental hypothesis resolving naturally. If it stabilizes or reverses, it may indicate hardware settling at new equilibrium. Maintaining regular measurement frequency is essential to characterize the resolution dynamics of whatever caused the post-baseline elevation.

state.question: What explains the sustained pattern of variation in my precision measurements across both pendulum and resonator systems over the baseline period?

hypotheses.label: Normal measurement variation within expected precision limits
hypotheses.rationale: 42 pendulum trials show values ranging from 1.6445 to 1.6995 beats (span ~3.3%), with most clustering near the mean of 1.6691. 18 resonator trials range from 2.6758 to 2.7350 cycles/beat (span ~2.2%). For experimental apparatus in a new settlement environment, this degree of scatter around stable means is consistent with ordinary measurement uncertainty from temperature fluctuations, vibration, timing precision limits, and human factors in observation. No systematic drift is evident. Both instruments appear to be performing as precision instruments should during a baseline establishment phase.

hypotheses.label: Uncontrolled environmental variables affecting both systems
hypotheses.rationale: If temperature, pressure, or local gravitational variations were meaningfully affecting measurements, I would expect correlated changes across both systems. However, the data show no obvious correlation pattern between pendulum and resonator variations on the same days. Day 5 shows resonator values below mean while day 8 shows them above, but corresponding pendulum data from adjacent days show no parallel pattern. Environmental factors remain possible contributors to the observed scatter but are not supported as a dominant systematic effect.

hypotheses.label: Instrument calibration drift requiring correction
hypotheses.rationale: True drift would manifest as a temporal trend. Examining chronologically: pendulum trials show no monotonic increase or decrease from day 3 through day 10. The day 10 values (1.6687, 1.6785, 1.6827) are higher than day 7 values (1.6445, 1.6657, 1.6677) but not higher than day 4 peak (1.6995) or day 6 values (1.6928). Resonator similarly shows no clear temporal trend. This pattern is inconsistent with calibration drift.

beliefTimeline.summaryOfChange: First substantive review. The key recognition is that there is no anomaly requiring explanation — what I observe is precisely what baseline establishment should produce: stable means with typical measurement scatter. The 'question' reflects that I need to explain the pattern I see, and the dominant hypothesis (75%) is that this is normal instrument behavior. I maintain modest probability in environmental factors and calibration drift as due diligence, and reserve 5% residual for unconsidered alternatives. All 60 measurement events inform the assessment that both instruments are performing within expected precision bounds.

state.question: What explains the elevated resonator measurements in the post-baseline period (days 11-13) compared to the baseline period (days 1-10)?

hypotheses.label: Normal measurement variation within expected precision limits
hypotheses.rationale: The three post-baseline resonator trials (events 210, 211, 212) show mean 2.7283 cycles/beat vs baseline mean 2.7017, giving z=1.78. This is approaching but not exceeding the conventional 2-sigma threshold for statistical significance. With only n=3 post-baseline trials, this could represent ordinary sampling variation from the tail of the baseline distribution. Event 210 at 2.7714 is indeed the highest value recorded across all 21 trials, but event 139 during baseline showed 2.7350, demonstrating that elevated values occurred in the baseline period as well. However, the fact that 2 of 3 post-baseline values exceed the baseline mean, combined with the z-score, makes pure chance less probable than before.

hypotheses.label: Systematic environmental change affecting resonator after day 10
hypotheses.rationale: The post-baseline mean shift is borderline significant (z=1.78) and all three post-baseline measurements occurred on days 11-13. If temperature, humidity, or another environmental parameter changed systematically after the baseline period ended, this could produce the observed upward shift in resonator frequency. Critically, the pendulum shows NO corresponding shift (z=-0.04), which argues against a general gravitational or timing system change but is consistent with resonator-specific environmental sensitivity (e.g., to temperature affecting cavity dimensions or air density affecting acoustic properties). The lack of correlation between instruments actually supports different environmental sensitivities rather than refuting environmental causes.

hypotheses.label: Resonator calibration drift or physical change after day 10
hypotheses.rationale: A physical change to the resonator apparatus itself (mounting loosening, cavity deformation, acoustic coupling change) could produce an upward shift in measured frequency. Unlike gradual drift, this would explain a step-change pattern: baseline period stable, then elevated post-baseline. The timing coincides with the transition from baseline to post-baseline measurement schedule, which might have involved handling or repositioning the apparatus. However, I have not documented any maintenance, relocation, or physical intervention with the resonator that would explain such a change, making this less probable than environmental factors.

hypotheses.label: Measurement protocol or observer bias change coinciding with formal baseline end
hypotheses.rationale: If I unconsciously changed my measurement procedure or observation criteria when I formally designated day 10 as the end of baseline, this could introduce systematic bias. However, I maintain meticulous protocols specifically to prevent such effects, and the pendulum measurements show no corresponding change, suggesting my measurement discipline remained consistent across both instruments. This hypothesis has low prior probability given my methodological training.

beliefTimeline.summaryOfChange: QUESTION REPLACED: Previously focused on explaining variation within the baseline period (days 1-10), which I now recognize was normal measurement scatter around stable means. The real anomaly requiring explanation is the post-baseline resonator elevation (z=1.78) with no corresponding pendulum change. This is an unexplained pattern in collected data, not a continuation of baseline establishment. Rebuilt hypothesis set around this specific anomaly. Environmental change (0.40) and normal variation (0.35) are now co-leading hypotheses, with instrument change (0.20) as plausible alternative. The lack of pendulum correlation actually strengthens environmental explanations by suggesting instrument-specific sensitivity rather than refuting environmental causes generally.

state.question: What explains the resonator measurements showing elevated first-mode values in post-baseline trials (days 11-15) compared to baseline (days 1-10)?

hypotheses.label: Normal measurement variation within expected precision limits
hypotheses.rationale: The post-baseline mean (2.7164 cycles/beat, n=6) vs baseline mean (2.7017, n=18) gives z=1.30, which is below the 2-sigma threshold. However, examining the full post-baseline dataset now available (n=6 instead of n=3) shows sustained elevation: trials 19, 22 show notably high values (2.7714, 2.7304), while trials 20, 21, 23, 24 are closer to baseline. The z-score of 1.30 indicates this is plausible as sampling variation, but the persistence across 6 trials and presence of the highest-ever value (2.7714) makes pure chance less likely than initially assessed.

hypotheses.label: Systematic environmental change affecting resonator after day 10
hypotheses.rationale: The resonator shows z=1.30 upward shift post-baseline while pendulum shows z=-0.04 (essentially zero shift), indicating instrument-specific rather than general gravitational/timing effects. Environmental factors affecting resonator cavity (temperature, humidity, air density) would selectively impact acoustic measurements. The pattern shows two notably elevated values (events 210, 235) interspersed with near-baseline values, consistent with environmental fluctuation rather than step-change. Days 11-15 span sufficient time for environmental variation. This differential response between instruments strengthens environmental hypothesis.

hypotheses.label: Resonator calibration drift or physical change after day 10
hypotheses.rationale: A step-change in resonator physical properties (cavity deformation, mounting shift, acoustic coupling change) would explain why the shift appears instrument-specific. However, the post-baseline data shows variation rather than uniform elevation: events 236, 237 (day 15) actually show values below baseline mean (2.6959, 2.6872 vs 2.7017), inconsistent with permanent physical change. If hardware shifted on day 10-11, I would expect sustained elevation, not the pattern of high-low-high-low seen across days 13-15. This argues against fixed calibration drift and toward transient causes.

hypotheses.label: Measurement protocol or observer bias change at baseline transition
hypotheses.rationale: Pendulum measurements show no corresponding shift (z=-0.04), indicating my measurement discipline remained consistent across instruments. My protocols are designed to prevent observer-dependent changes. With n=6 post-baseline trials now showing internal variation rather than uniform bias, systematic observer error becomes even less probable.

beliefTimeline.summaryOfChange: Question retained as the resonator elevation pattern remains the primary anomaly. With n=6 post-baseline trials now available (vs n=3 previously), z-score decreased from 1.78 to 1.30, making normal variation MORE probable (0.35→0.25) but not dominant. Environmental hypothesis increased (0.40→0.45) as the sustained differential response between instruments and the fluctuating pattern (high on days 13,15; near-baseline on day 15 events 236-237) fits environmental variation better than fixed causes. Physical change hypothesis nearly unchanged (0.20→0.22) but rationale updated: late-period near-baseline values (events 236, 237) argue against permanent calibration shift. Observer bias remains low (0.03→0.02). The key insight: post-baseline data shows variation rather than uniform elevation, favoring transient environmental over fixed systematic causes.

state.question: What explains the resonator measurements showing elevated variance and occasional extreme values in post-baseline trials (days 11-18) compared to baseline (days 1-10)?

hypotheses.label: Normal measurement variation within expected precision limits
hypotheses.rationale: Full post-baseline dataset (n=12, days 11-18) now shows mean 2.7104 vs baseline 2.7017, giving z=0.97, well below 2-sigma threshold. This shift is statistically unremarkable. However, the distribution shows notably increased variance: event 210 yielded 2.7714 (highest ever recorded, >3 sigma above baseline mean), while events 236, 237, 274, 275 show values below baseline mean. This high-low pattern with extreme outlier is less consistent with simple sampling variation from a stable process.

hypotheses.label: Environmental fluctuations affecting resonator cavity properties after day 10
hypotheses.rationale: Resonator shows z=0.97 shift with high variance while pendulum shows z=-0.04 (essentially unchanged), confirming instrument-specific rather than general timing effect. Acoustic resonance is sensitive to temperature, humidity, and air density. The pattern across days 11-18 shows alternating high and low values rather than monotonic drift: day 13 has extreme high (2.7714) alongside normal values; days 15, 17, 18 show multiple below-baseline measurements. This fluctuation pattern is characteristic of environmental variation rather than fixed calibration shift. Extended post-baseline period (8 days) provides sufficient time for environmental cycling.

hypotheses.label: Intermittent resonator hardware issue beginning around day 13
hypotheses.rationale: Event 210 (day 13, 2.7714 cycles/beat) represents an outlier >3 sigma above baseline mean, occurring after days 11-12 showed only modest elevation. If this were environmental or sampling variation, such an extreme value would be extraordinarily unlikely. Subsequent measurements returned to reasonable range (events 211, 212 on same day), suggesting transient rather than permanent change. Days 15-18 show continued variance but no repeat of the extreme event 210 value. Pattern is consistent with intermittent issue (loose connection, mounting vibration, acoustic interference) that manifested most severely on day 13. However, the issue appears self-correcting or sporadic rather than progressive.

hypotheses.label: Measurement protocol change or observer bias at baseline transition
hypotheses.rationale: Pendulum measurements show no shift (z=-0.04), indicating consistent measurement discipline across instruments. My protocols are designed to eliminate observer-dependent variation. The 12 post-baseline trials show internal variation inconsistent with systematic observer bias, which would produce uniform shift.

beliefTimeline.summaryOfChange: Question refined from 'elevated first-mode values in days 11-15' to 'elevated variance and occasional extreme values in days 11-18' to reflect the full dataset now available (n=12 post-baseline trials vs n=6 previously). The extended data reveals the pattern is increased variance rather than simple mean shift (z=0.97, not significant), with event 210 standing out as genuine outlier. Probability mass shifted: 'normal variation' decreased 0.25→0.15 due to the extreme event 210 value; 'environmental fluctuations' increased 0.45→0.50 as the high-variance, alternating pattern across 8 days strengthens this explanation; new hypothesis 'intermittent hardware issue' introduced at 0.25 to explain the day-13 outlier specifically; 'calibration drift' hypothesis retired because days 15-18 show values both above AND below baseline, incompatible with fixed shift.

state.question: What explains the resonator measurements showing elevated variance and a statistically significant mean shift (z=1.34) in post-baseline trials (days 11-20, n=15) compared to baseline (days 1-10, n=18)?

hypotheses.label: Normal measurement variation within expected precision limits
hypotheses.rationale: The full post-baseline dataset now spans days 11-20 (n=15) and shows mean 2.7129 vs baseline 2.7017, yielding z=1.34. While still below 2-sigma threshold for claiming statistical significance by conventional standards, this is notably higher than the z=0.97 observed through day 18. The drift is now approaching marginal significance. More importantly, the variance remains elevated with both extreme highs (event 210: 2.7714) and consistent below-baseline values (events 236, 237, 274, 275). A z=1.34 shift combined with high variance is less consistent with simple sampling from a stable process. Additionally, pendulum remains stable at z=-0.04, suggesting the resonator pattern is not random noise.

hypotheses.label: Environmental fluctuations affecting resonator cavity properties after day 10
hypotheses.rationale: Resonator now shows z=1.34 upward shift while pendulum shows z=-0.04, confirming instrument-specific effect. The pattern across days 11-20 continues to show fluctuation rather than monotonic drift: day 13 extreme high (2.7714), days 15-18 mixed high-low, days 20 returning to moderately elevated (events 299-301: mean ~2.72). This non-monotonic pattern with both elevated and depressed values is characteristic of environmental cycling (temperature, humidity, air density affecting acoustic resonance). The slight upward mean shift (z=1.34) could represent seasonal or facility-level environmental change establishing a new equilibrium with higher variance. Day 20 measurements cluster around 2.71-2.74, suggesting possible stabilization at elevated level. This remains the most parsimonious explanation for instrument-specific variance without hardware failure indicators.

hypotheses.label: Intermittent resonator hardware issue beginning around day 13
hypotheses.rationale: Event 210 (day 13, 2.7714) remains the most extreme outlier at >3 sigma above baseline mean. However, subsequent days have not reproduced this extreme value. Days 15-18 showed elevated variance but values mostly in 2.68-2.73 range. Day 20 (events 299-301) shows relatively tight clustering around 2.71-2.74, suggesting no progressive hardware degradation. If hardware issue were present, I would expect either: (a) recurring extreme values like event 210, or (b) progressive drift. Neither pattern is evident. The isolated nature of event 210 and subsequent stabilization (even if at slightly elevated mean) argues against persistent hardware fault. However, I cannot fully exclude intermittent issue that manifested once severely and otherwise contributes to elevated variance.

hypotheses.label: Measurement protocol change or observer bias at baseline transition
hypotheses.rationale: Pendulum measurements remain stable (z=-0.04) across the same period, demonstrating consistent measurement discipline. No protocol changes were implemented. Day 20 measurements were conducted with same protocols as day 11. Observer bias would produce systematic shift, not the high-variance pattern observed.

beliefTimeline.summaryOfChange: Updated question to reflect strengthened statistical pattern: z-score increased from 0.97 (through day 18) to 1.34 (through day 20), approaching marginal significance. Decreased probability of normal variation from 0.15 to 0.05 because z=1.34 combined with persistent variance is less consistent with stable process sampling. Increased environmental fluctuations from 0.50 to 0.55 as day 20 data shows clustering around elevated mean (2.71-2.74), suggesting possible stabilization at new environmental equilibrium. Maintained hardware issue at 0.25 but noted day 20 clustering argues against progressive degradation. Protocol/bias remains minimal at 0.02. Increased residual from 0.08 to 0.13 to acknowledge growing statistical significance demands consideration of explanations not yet formulated.

state.question: What explains the resonator measurements showing sustained elevated mean (z=1.50 over all post-baseline data, days 11-23) and persistent high variance compared to baseline (days 1-10)?

hypotheses.label: Environmental fluctuations affecting resonator cavity properties after day 10
hypotheses.rationale: Resonator now shows z=1.50 upward shift over full post-baseline period (n=21, days 11-23) while pendulum remains stable at z=-0.04, confirming instrument-specific effect. The pattern continues to show non-monotonic fluctuation: extreme high on day 13 (event 210: 2.7714), mixed values days 15-18, elevated clustering days 20-22 (events 299-301, 324-326 mostly in 2.71-2.74 range), and day 23 (events 328-330) showing continued high variance (2.6704 to 2.7432). This sustained pattern of elevated mean with high variance, without progressive drift or repeated extreme outliers, is most consistent with environmental factors (temperature, humidity, air pressure) affecting acoustic resonance properties. The fact that variance remains high but values cluster around a new elevated equilibrium (roughly 2.71-2.74 in recent days) suggests stable environmental shift rather than transient fluctuation. Increased probability from 0.55 because z-score has grown to 1.50 and pattern has persisted for 13 days without reverting to baseline.

hypotheses.label: Normal measurement variation within expected precision limits
hypotheses.rationale: The z=1.50 shift is now approaching conventional 2-sigma threshold and has persisted across 21 post-baseline measurements over 13 days. While still technically below strict significance threshold, the combination of sustained elevated mean, high variance, and instrument-specificity (pendulum stable) makes random sampling from baseline distribution increasingly implausible. Recent days (22-23) continue to show values predominantly above baseline mean (events 324, 325, 329 all >2.70), inconsistent with random fluctuation. Decreased from 0.05.

hypotheses.label: Intermittent resonator hardware issue beginning around day 13
hypotheses.rationale: Event 210 (2.7714) remains a significant outlier. However, across days 20-23 (9 additional measurements), no similar extreme values have appeared. Day 23 shows wide range (event 330: 2.6704 to event 329: 2.7432) but this variance pattern without repeated extremes or progressive degradation argues against persistent hardware fault. If intermittent electronic or mechanical issue exists, it would more likely produce recurring spikes or gradual drift. The sustained slight elevation with variance could involve subtle hardware change (e.g., mounting stress, thermal expansion of cavity) that isn't progressive failure. Cannot fully exclude, but 13 days without reproducing the extreme outlier reduces probability. Decreased from 0.25.

hypotheses.label: Measurement protocol change or observer bias at baseline transition
hypotheses.rationale: Pendulum continues stable (z=-0.04) through day 12, demonstrating consistent measurement discipline. No protocol changes implemented. The high variance in resonator (ranging from 2.6704 to 2.7432 in recent days) is inconsistent with systematic observer bias, which would produce consistent shift.
